title: The popular version. Franklin ran his days to a strict timetable.
description:
Franklin ran his days to a strict timetable. The timetable is real. It is in his autobiography.

Up at five. Asleep at ten. It opened with a question: "What good shall I do this day?" It closed with another: "What good have I done to day?"

"My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble." Order was the virtue that asked every part of his business to have its allotted time.

He told a story about a speckled ax. A man tires of polishing it and accepts it while it is still only speckled. Franklin admits he was tempted the same way.

He never arrived at the perfection he sought. But he judged himself "a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been".

The famous schedule was a target, not a record.

Sources:
- https://ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography/page40.htm (read): Franklin's Autobiography text with his daily schedule: "The Morning Question, What good Shall I do this Day?", "Rise, wash, and address Powerful Goodness" at 5, evening activities ending with "Examination of the Day", "Evening Question, What Good have I done to day?", and "Sleep" at 10; the precept of Order requires that every part of his business should have its allotted time.
- https://ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography/page41.htm (read): Franklin writes "My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble"; tells the story of the man who accepts an ax that is only speckled; admits he never arrived at the perfection he sought but was "a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been".
- https://ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography/page38.htm (read): the Order precept as worded: "Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time."
